claims.text: Frege introduced modern quantificational logic in the Begriffsschrift of 1879, devising a formal language with quantifier symbols binding variables, together with axioms and rules of inference, in what amounts to a presentation of first-order predicate logic.

source.title: Frege, G., Begriffsschrift, eine der arithmetischen nachgebildete Formelsprache des reinen Denkens, 1879

claims.text: Frege did not introduce the now-standard symbols. His universal quantifier was written as a concavity in a two-dimensional notation; the modern universal symbol is due to Gentzen and the existential to Peano. Contemporaries found the two-dimensional notation difficult and largely failed to see its advantages over Boole’s approach.

source.title: Frege, G., Begriffsschrift, eine der arithmetischen nachgebildete Formelsprache des reinen Denkens, 1879

claims.text: Frege officially adopts only one rule of inference, modus ponens, while tacitly making use of a rule of instantiation for the universal quantifier.

source.title: Frege, G., Begriffsschrift, eine der arithmetischen nachgebildete Formelsprache des reinen Denkens, 1879

claims.text: Priority is contested: scholars of Peirce note that the Begriffsschrift is among the first published accounts of a logical system with quantification rather than being uniquely the first.

source.title: Frege, G., Begriffsschrift, eine der arithmetischen nachgebildete Formelsprache des reinen Denkens, 1879

beats.broke: ordinary language cannot express the difference between one thing working for everybody and everybody having something of their own, and the two are different requirements
beats.fix: bind variables explicitly, so the order of the quantifiers is written down rather than left to the reader
beats.cost: the notation is unambiguous and unreadable, which is why it took decades to be adopted even by logicians
beats.interview: what changes when you swap the order of two quantifiers
